name: Recency effect
statement: The last items in a list are recalled best, and in immediate free recall thirty seconds of filled delay removes that advantage.
meaning: Ask someone to recall a list in any order and plot accuracy against the position each word held. The curve bows up at both ends. The rise at the end is the recency effect, and the smaller rise at the start is primacy. Recency is the larger of the two in immediate free recall, and it is the part that a filled delay destroys. That fragility is why the effect was read for decades as a readout from a short-term store holding the last few items. The reading is now disputed, because recency returns when a distractor task is placed between every item as well as after the last one. Two separate claims travel under the one name. The first is this memory finding, which holds in almost every participant tested. The second is a claim about judgement, that raters, auditors and investors weight recent information too heavily, and it rests on a thinner and more mixed literature.

origin.note: Murdock's paper is the one the field cites for the free-recall serial position curve, but the curve was already in the literature: Glanzer and Cunitz's reference list carries Deese and Kaufman's 1957 serial-effects paper and Raffel on primacy from 1936. The mechanism paper is Glanzer and Cunitz in 1966, which separated the two ends of the curve by manipulating each independently.

evidence: Glanzer and Cunitz ran the two experiments that made the curve into an argument. In the first, 240 Army enlisted men heard eight 20-word lists at one word every 3, 6 or 9 seconds. Slower presentation raised recall across the first fifteen positions and did nothing to the last five. Summing correct responses in blocks of five gave F of 23.46, 16.21 and 22.00 for the first three blocks, all p < .001 on 2 and 235 degrees of freedom. For the last block F was 1.71, p > .10. In the second, 46 enlisted men saw fifteen 15-word lists and were then shown either a cross-hatch, meaning write, or a digit, meaning count aloud from that number until told to write. Ten seconds of counting removed most of the end peak and thirty seconds left no trace of it. Delay was significant only in the last five positions, F(1,45) = 22.42, p < .001, against F = 3.60, p > .05, for the first five and F = 1.44, p > .10, for the second five. A pilot using thirty seconds of empty delay with no task did cut the end peak, F(1,233) = 37.00, p < .001, but a clear end peak survived, which is why the counting task was added. A footnote records Postman and Phillips reporting similar results in 1965. Bjork and Whitten then broke the explanation. Twenty paid undergraduates at Michigan studied four lists of ten word pairs, with 12 seconds of arithmetic before and after every pair and 20 seconds after the last one. Both primacy and recency appeared anyway. Forty more undergraduates saw four kinds of list. On lists with no interpolated arithmetic, adding 30 seconds of arithmetic before recall flattened recency, as Glanzer and Cunitz had found. On lists with 12 seconds of arithmetic around every pair, the same 30 seconds did nothing to the recency portion of the curve. A word in the latter lists waited seven times as long for recall as its counterpart in an immediate list, and recall was about the same at every position except the last few.

replication.headline: Healey and Kahana gave 126 people 112 lists each and found that 90% of them showed recency individually, not merely in the group average.
replication.detail: The concern with a curve of this kind is that averaging hides people who did something else. Healey and Kahana tested it on the Penn Electrophysiology of Encoding and Retrieval Study, 126 participants aged 17 to 30, each studying 112 lists of 16 words for immediate free recall. Defining recency as higher mean recall across the final six positions than across positions 5 to 10, 90% of participants showed it on both no-task and task lists. Defining primacy as higher recall for items 1 to 4 than for mid-list positions, 93% showed that. Recall started at the final item for 64% of participants on no-task lists and 79% on task lists, and average initiation probability for mid-list items was under 1%. The task manipulation there is a size or animacy judgement made during study, not a distractor before recall, so every list was an immediate test. What has not survived intact is the explanation. Thapar and Greene report that substantial recency remained when a different distractor task followed every list position, which they read as evidence against the short-term store. Davelaar and colleagues argue the opposite way from the same literature: short-term and long-term recency have different properties, and two components are needed, an episodic contextual system plus an activation-based buffer. So the effect replicates and the mechanism is open.

study.cite: Healey, M. K., & Kahana, M. J. (2014). Is memory search governed by universal principles or idiosyncratic strategies? Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(2), 575-596.

limits: Nothing above is an effect size, and none of these papers reports one. The memory literature here quantifies recency as recall probability by position and as the proportion of people showing the pattern, so the structured effect-size fields are empty rather than filled with a number no source contains. The applied claim is the weaker half of this entry by a wide margin. Hogarth and Einhorn's belief-adjustment model, five experiments and 192 adults, predicts recency for short simple series processed step by step, and that description is read from the ERIC record because the paper is paywalled. Steiner and Rain manipulated where a single good or poor performance fell among average ones. Study 1 used 333 undergraduates watching four videotaped lectures. Its abstract breaks off mid-sentence after reporting a recency effect for overall ratings, so nothing further from it is quoted. Trotman and Wright reviewed the auditing literature on order effects in 2000 and their own summary is that the results are mixed and stayed mixed after two more studies. On the finance side, Greenwood and Shleifer regressed six survey measures of expected stock returns on the past twelve months of returns and the price level, average R-squared 0.40 across the six. The coefficient on past returns was positive and significant for four of the six surveys. It was not significant for the Graham-Harvey series, t = 1.377, and it was negative and not significant for the Shiller series, minus 1.878 at t = minus 0.205. Those figures come from the NBER working-paper version, which is what could be opened, and the published article may renumber its tables. Murdock's 1962 paper is paywalled and its full text was not obtained; what appears above about it comes from the sentence Glanzer and Cunitz devote to its presentation-rate conditions and from a truncated abstract record. Thapar and Greene and Davelaar and colleagues were read from abstracts only. Searches covered Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, ERIC and web search, and no meta-analysis of the serial position effect was located.
misreadings: The commonest error is the textbook one. Most pages that explain recency say it is items still sitting in short-term memory, and offer the thirty-second distractor as proof. That manipulation works only in the immediate paradigm. Put a distractor between every item as well as at the end and recency comes back, which is what Bjork and Whitten found and what Thapar and Greene confirmed against the obvious objection. The short-term store may still be part of the answer, and Davelaar and colleagues argue it is, but a page that presents the buffer as settled is a page that stopped reading in 1968. The second error is transfer. The memory effect is close to universal, at 90% of individuals in the Penn sample, and the judgement claim called recency bias in management and investing writing is a different assertion with its own much weaker record. Auditing researchers who tested it directly describe their own results as mixed. Robustness in one does not carry to the other. The third error is treating recency as the whole curve. Primacy appeared in 93% of the same participants, and in Glanzer and Cunitz the two ends respond to opposite manipulations: slower presentation lifts the start and leaves the end alone, filled delay flattens the end and leaves the start alone. The last error is scale. Healey and Kahana put it as a ratio: recency depends on the gap between successive items relative to the gap between the last item and recall. So recency is not a fixed span of items, and it survives long delays when the spacing is stretched to match.

Bjork, R. A., & Whitten, W. B. (1974). Recency-sensitive retrieval processes in long-term free recall. Cognitive Psychology, 6(2), 173-189. Read in full from the scan hosted by the Bjork Learning and Forgetting Lab.

Postman, L., & Phillips, L. W. (1965). Short-term temporal changes in free recall. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 17(2), 132-138. Cited by Glanzer and Cunitz as reporting similar results; not read here.

Deese, J., & Kaufman, R. A. (1957). Serial effects in recall of unorganized and sequentially organized verbal material. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 54(3), 180-187. Named here as an antecedent on the strength of Glanzer and Cunitz's reference list; not read.
